title: Connexions de Gauss-Manin et équations de Picard-Fuchs. Opération de Cartier : copies de tapuscrit annoté (s.d.), tiré à part (1981), notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting. X/S is a smooth family, essentially a family of curves, over a smooth base S. There is a Picard–Fuchs operator D = Σ_i D_i ω_i, a differential operator on S acting on relative 1-forms or classes ω_i, which kills the de Rham class: Σ ∇(D_i)[ω_i] = 0 in H^1_dR(X/S). Locally this means Σ \bar D_i ω'_i = d_{X/S} φ for a function φ on X; this is presumably formula (10). For two sections a, b of X → S, the 'abelian integral with moving endpoints' s ↦ ∫_{a(s)}^{b(s)} ω_s is a multivalued analytic function. Applying D to it gives a single-valued function μ(a,b) on S. This is the inhomogeneous term of the Picard–Fuchs equation, i.e. the Manin map. By (5) it is additive: μ(a,b)+μ(b,c) = μ(a,c).

The previous page establishes (15): D_s ∫_{Z_s} ω'_s = ∫_{Z_s} (\bar D ω')_s for horizontal families of cycles Z_s. This is the 'transcendental' compatibility of the algebraic Gauss–Manin connection with differentiation of periods.

This page:
(i) Remark. (15) gives a check that the relations satisfied by the periods (∫_{γ_i} ω) are exactly the Picard–Fuchs relations. This follows from de Rham's theorem on the fibres X_s.
(ii) New section: 'computing μ(a,b) algebraically, without integrals'.
  - By the cocycle relation (5), one reduces to the case where a(s_0) and b(s_0) are close, chaining through intermediate local sections.
  - Then, locally near s_0, X/S admits an integrable connection, i.e. a flat lifting of vector fields (a local analytic trivialization).
  - One may choose this connection so that a and b are horizontal.
  - Then differentiation under the integral gives (14): μ(a,b) = φ(b(s)) − φ(a(s)), with φ the primitive from (10). So μ is the difference of the values of the 'Picard–Fuchs primitive' at the two points.
(iii) He then wants a formula without assuming a, b horizontal. This is started at the bottom and continued on the next page: compare with horizontal sections a_0, b_0 through a(s_0), b(s_0). The correction terms D ∫_{b_0}^{b} ω and D ∫_{a_0}^{a} ω are purely local and are to be expressed via pullbacks a^*(ω).

Aim: an algebraic description of the Manin homomorphism, as in Manin's 1963 proof of Mordell over function fields, through the Gauss–Manin connection.
errors: The reduction to 'a(s_0), b(s_0) close' uses intermediate sections and local (analytic or étale) trivializations, so the resulting formula is only local. Global algebraicity of μ must come from the cocycle and uniqueness, not from (14) directly. This is not spelled out.

The step 'one can choose the connection so that a and b are horizontal' is fine locally analytically (take a trivialization sending a, b to constant sections), but it is not algebraic. φ is also only defined locally, up to an additive constant, which cancels in φ(b) − φ(a). Implicit but correct.
The independence of (14) from the choice of connection and of φ is not checked on this page.

ideas.what: D applied to ∫_{a(s)}^{b(s)} ω gives a single-valued function μ(a,b), additive in (a,b)
ideas.modern_name: Manin map / Manin homomorphism (inhomogeneous Picard–Fuchs equation)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Yu. Manin (1963); clarified by Coleman (1990), Chai (1991)

ideas.what: Compatibility D_s ∫_{Z_s} ω = ∫_{Z_s} ∇_D ω via de Rham's theorem on fibres
ideas.where_published: Ideas present in Grothendieck's 'On the de Rham cohomology of algebraic varieties' (1966) context; unsure about explicit statement

ideas.what: Local computation μ(a,b) = φ(b) − φ(a), with φ a primitive of the Picard–Fuchs-annihilated form, using horizontal sections
ideas.modern_name: Explicit formula for the Manin map via a primitive of D(ω) (cf. Coleman's computation)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Manin; Coleman 1990 'Manin's proof of the Mordell conjecture over function fields'

missed.claim: Grothendieck sets out to give an explicit formula for the Manin map for arbitrary, non-horizontal sections, as a local algebraic expression involving a^*(ω). The thread is started on this and the next page and marked 'donner une formule....!', apparently left unfinished. Later work (Coleman, Chai, Bertrand) achieves comparable explicit descriptions, so the content is largely recovered in the literature, though not credited to him.
missed.quote: Il y aurait lieu d'expliciter aussi une formule explicite, sans supposer que a(s) et b(s) soient horizontales.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mainly historical: it documents Grothendieck working on an algebraic treatment of the Manin map (c. 1972), predating Coleman's 1990 clarification of gaps in Manin's argument.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard local computation of the Manin map via Gauss–Manin. The content is known (Manin, Coleman, Chai). It is of historical interest only as Grothendieck's unpublished engagement with it.
transcription_corrections: Line 2: the inserted text above 'calcul d'intégrales' is plausibly 'c'est local mais' (uncertain); the machine reading 'c'est-à-dire' is doubtful.
'(14)' is written above 'trouve' as the equation label for μ(a,b) = φ(b(s)) − φ(a(s)).
Line 2 of the page: the pair is likely '(∫_{γ_i}, φ(s_i))' or similar period expressions; the reading is uncertain.
